extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers of 19th-century American literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive remarks about poetic and prose craft embedded in a satirical poem—guidance on sonnet form, unity, diction, ornament, originality, rhythm, and the balance between passion and polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnets: unity and cumulative force
rubrics_metrics.description: A sonnet should 'reach with one impulse the end of its course' so that 'not a verse should be salient, but each one should tend / With a wave-like up-gathering to break at the end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense strength here, smooth a wry kink; the sonnet's effect is a single impulse that gathers and breaks at the close—avoid lines that stand out awkwardly or interrupt the cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and the organic wholeness of a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem's power lies in 'the general tone, the something pervading, uniting the whole'—removing small parts can take away a 'chief limb of the statue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the pervading, unifying quality that makes disparate parts cohere; don't treat good lines as interchangeable fragments to be jumbled without regard to overall tone and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of obscure classical allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet warns of an 'ankle-deep' mire 'of deliberate confusion, / Made up of old jumbles of classic allusion' and implies such excess produces dulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from piling recondite or gratuitous classical references that confuse readers; omit dull or excessive learned allusions that do not serve clarity or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author apologizes for 'many digressions' and notes it is 'so hard to escape if you get in their mesh once.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the reader's focus: excessive wandering weakens a piece. If digressions must occur, manage them deliberately and sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surface imitation; copy substance, not mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators 'omit no part of the man but his wisdom and wit' and 'mirror his mists and obscurities'—superficial mimicry lacks the original's true qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reproduce only the external traits of another writer; strive for original thought and insight rather than echoing mannerisms that leave out what made the model powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-ornament 'ruins both poem and prose'—excessive conceits and pet phrases can obscure merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornamentation with restraint; when prose or poetry runs free and unforced it often reads better than when laden with affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture spontaneity; avoid overworking immediate inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 'best things are done in the flush of the moment; if he wait, all is spoiled...the fixed air once gone, he can never re-make it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a creative moment yields a striking passage, recognize the risk that revising or delaying may dissipate its life; balance revision with preserving immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure written work stands apart from oral performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer 'talks he is great, but goes out like a taper, / If you shut him up closely with pen, ink, and paper'—oral brilliance does not guarantee written power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop craft specifically for the page: sustain voice, structure, and clarity in writing rather than relying on spoken charm or delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance polish with passion; avoid over-smoothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much polish can 'hang any zeal' and leave the work lacking in enthusiasm—'He is too smooth and too polished to hang any zeal on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance where technical refinement does not extinguish emotional force; polish should enhance, not cool, the work's energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control fervor; preserve craft (grammar, rhyme) and avoid repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fervent poets may 'know no separation 'twixt simple excitement and pure inspiration,' leading to grammatical lapses, faulty rhymes, and repeated lyrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harness passionate energy with editorial discipline: check grammar and rhyme, pare repetitive phrases, and ensure the heat of inspiration does not excuse sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perfectionist paralysis; produce rather than endlessly plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic describes someone who 'so well all that makes up good poetry knows, / That the best of his poems is written in prose' and who 'loiters debating'—spending life 'learning to swim on his library table.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let analysis or over-knowledge of craft prevent creating finished works; move from knowing how to do something to actually doing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice restraint and maturation; avoid premature, noisy production
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasty authors 'must pelt down an unripe and colicky crop' and 'strip themselves naked to prove he's a poet'—too soon is as bad as too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow work to mature; favor measured, balanced development over flashy, premature displays of force or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating one successful device or character poorly
rubrics_metrics.description: An author 'has drawn you one character...He has done naught but copy it ill ever since'—recycling a single success leads to deterioration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overuse or poorly rework a single striking invention; strive for variety and authentic development rather than repeated caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythmic force and directness in prose and sermons
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful prose can have periods that 'fall on you, stroke after stroke, / Like the blows of a lumberer felling an oak'—direct, forceful rhythm is an advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythm and blunt, driving cadences where appropriate to achieve rhetorical impact; vigor and clarity can be virtues in prose as well as verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let prose run natural and unforced rather than twitchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of a writer who 'twitches and jerks so'—when prose slips free it 'runs like a stream with a musical waste.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for fluid, natural phrasing in prose; excessive stunting, contrivance, or artificial ticks disrupt reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value national originality rather than slavish foreign imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem satirizes the tendency to accuse 'every national author a poor one, / That isn't a copy of something that's foreign' and to court English notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate authentic national or personal voices instead of seeking validation by copying foreign models; originality trumps slavish deference to external fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and care in plotting—avoid overly slender or slippery plots
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker calls his own plot 'slender and slippery'—a plot that is 'more slender, and likely to slip awry' can frustrate readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain enough substance and structural security in plot so the narrative does not dissolve; slenderness may be acceptable but requires careful control to avoid collapse.
